summary: Describes version 1 of the Network Time Protocol (NTP) and gives its structure and implementation information. NTP synchronizes clocks across a hierarchy of time servers and keeps time accurate to within tens of milliseconds in most of the Internet. It replaces RFC 958 and was replaced by RFC 1119 and RFC 1305.

eli5.summary: Computers' clocks drift apart. NTP lets them ask more accurate clocks what time it is and adjust, so they all agree.

questions: how do computers synchronize their clocks
how does ntp handle clock drift
subtitle: The first synchronization protocol for accurate timekeeping across the Internet.

tldr.problem: Computers' clocks drift apart over time, but many network applications need to agree on the current time within a small tolerance. Manual synchronization is impractical at scale.
tldr.mechanism: NTPv1 uses a hierarchical master-slave architecture where systems exchange time information via UDP packets. Each system measures the offset between its clock and reference clocks, filters the measurements, and selects the best source to adjust its logical clock.
tldr.outcome: The protocol demonstrated that timekeeping accuracy within tens of milliseconds is achievable across the Internet using adaptive polling and error estimation. It was replaced by RFC 1119 and RFC 1305, which refined the design.

today: RFC 1059 has been obsoleted by RFC 1119 and RFC 1305, which introduced NTPv2 and NTPv3. NTPv1 is not used in modern networks, but the hierarchical synchronization architecture and the algorithmic approaches it pioneered remain central to NTP implementations today.

sections.title: The Network Time Protocol
sections.content:
NTPv1, defined in RFC 1059, is a protocol for synchronizing the clocks of computers across the Internet. It addresses a fundamental problem: computer clocks drift over time and disagree with each other, but many applications—from transaction logging to scientific measurement—require clocks to be within a small tolerance of each other and of a single authoritative time.

The protocol uses UDP as its transport layer and is built on a returnable-time design, meaning it measures time offsets by observing round-trip delays between communicating systems without requiring reliable message delivery. A system sends a message containing its local time; the peer returns the message; and the sender uses the receive and transmit timestamps to calculate how much the peer's clock differs from its own.
sections.eli5: NTPv1 is a system that lets computers ask each other what time it is and adjust their clocks. It works like calling a friend to check if you're wearing your watch right.

sections.title: Hierarchical Master-Slave Architecture
sections.content:
NTPv1 organizes time servers into a hierarchy using the concept of stratum. A primary time server (stratum 1) is synchronized to a national time standard via radio clock or other external reference. Secondary servers at stratum 2 synchronize themselves to stratum-1 servers. Servers at stratum 3 synchronize to stratum-2 servers, and so on. This hierarchical organization mimics the telephone industry's approach to timing distribution.

The protocol uses a minimum-weight spanning tree algorithm, derived from Bellman-Ford routing, to organize the synchronization paths automatically. When a primary server fails, the system reconfigures itself to use available secondary servers. If all primary servers become unavailable, secondary servers continue operating using their last known offset and frequency estimates, maintaining accuracy to within tens of milliseconds for extended periods. The synchronization distance—the measured round-trip delay between a server and its primary reference source—guides this automatic reconfiguration.
sections.eli5: Time servers are arranged in levels, like a pyramid. The top level has super-accurate clocks synchronized to radio. Each level below gets its time from the level above, making a chain. If one stops working, the system rearranges itself to use whatever works.

sections.title: Protocol Messages and State
sections.content:
NTPv1 uses a single message format transmitted over UDP port 123. Each message is built from several types of state variables: system variables (the local clock, current stratum, leap-second indicator), peer variables (data about each remote peer being synchronized), and packet variables (the actual message contents). Key packet fields include the leap indicator (warning of an impending leap second), version number (1 for NTPv1), stratum, polling interval, precision, synchronization distance, reference clock identifier, and timestamps.

Timestamps are the protocol's most critical data. NTPv1 represents time as a 64-bit fixed-point number: the first 32 bits hold the integer seconds since 1 January 1900, and the last 32 bits hold fractional seconds. This gives a precision of about 0.2 nanoseconds. When a client sends a message, it includes the local time at transmission. The server responds with the receive and transmit times, allowing the client to compute both the round-trip delay and the offset between clocks.
sections.eli5: Every message is like a postcard with timestamps written on it—when it left, when it arrived, when it's being sent back. By comparing these times, the receiving computer can figure out how much its clock is wrong and by how much the message delayed.

sections.title: Clock Filtering and Selection
sections.content:
Raw clock offset measurements from the network are noisy due to variable delays in network paths. NTPv1 addresses this with a clock filter algorithm that keeps a window of recent measurements (typically eight samples) and produces delay, offset, and dispersion estimates. The filter gives more weight to samples with smaller delays, preferring measurements that likely arrived with less network jitter. A selection algorithm then chooses which peer's offset estimate to use for adjusting the local clock.

The selection algorithm is designed to identify and reject falsetickers—clocks that are unreliable or broken—without requiring authentication or a voting majority. It uses statistical clustering to identify clocks that agree with each other. The algorithm is adaptive: if multiple reliable peers are available, it selects the one with the smallest synchronization distance. This voting approach is robust enough to handle cases where one or more peers are sending corrupted or incorrect time data.
sections.eli5: The protocol takes many measurements from different clocks and picks the ones that make the most sense. If most clocks agree and one is way off, the protocol ignores the odd one out—like knowing one person is lying when everyone else tells the same story.

sections.title: Logical Clock Discipline
sections.content:
Once NTPv1 has determined the best clock offset, it must adjust the local hardware clock to reduce this offset to zero. Rather than abruptly jumping the clock forward or backward—which breaks applications that expect time to move monotonically—the protocol uses a logical clock with slewing and drift-compensation mechanisms. A slew adjustment slowly nudges the clock's rate of advancement, while drift compensation accounts for the hardware oscillator's long-term frequency error.

The logical clock process, inspired by the Fuzzball routing platform, reads the offset estimate from the selected peer, compares it with the local clock's current frequency estimate, and applies phase and frequency corrections. These mechanisms can maintain accuracy to within a millisecond even after the system has lost synchronization to primary reference sources for many hours. The process runs continuously, adapting the clock's speed based on recent measurements of its drift.
sections.eli5: Instead of suddenly changing the time—which would confuse programs—the protocol slowly adjusts how fast the clock ticks. It's like gently turning up the speed of a record player to match what a metronome is playing, rather than stopping and restarting it.

fields.name: Leap Indicator
fields.desc: Warning of impending leap second insertion or deletion

fields.name: Stratum
fields.desc: Synchronization level; 1 is primary, higher numbers are secondary

fields.name: Poll Interval
fields.desc: Polling rate as a power of two in seconds

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: Clock precision as a power of two in seconds

fields.name: Synchronization Distance
fields.desc: Roundtrip delay to primary reference source

fields.name: Estimated Drift
fields.desc: Estimated frequency error of the local clock

fields.name: Reference ID
fields.desc: ID of reference clock or upstream server

fields.name: Reference Timestamp
fields.desc: Time the local clock was last adjusted

fields.name: Originate Timestamp
fields.desc: Time the sender created the message

fields.name: Transmit Timestamp
fields.desc: Time the message is being sent
